true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible null resource passed to policy store when all-clients resource is missing

When the client-specific resource is not found, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately passes the result to authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource is not found by name (e.g. realms where the admin-permissions resource server predates this change and was never re-initialized with the 'Clients' resource, since init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null). Existing deployments upgrading to a version with this schema change will not have the 'Clients' resource/scopes created, so this can produce a NullPointerException (or store-specific failure) on every client permission check instead of a clean deny, and the new Clients scopes/resources are never provisioned for existing realms.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same null-handling bug: getResourceTypeResource can return null, and passing that result directly to findByResource can cause a NullPointerException. Its additional upgrade-related explanation does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: unused getEvaluationContext, logger and TOKEN_EXCHANGE import

ClientPermissionsV2 contains a private getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) method that is never called (the only caller would be canExchangeTo, which now throws UnsupportedOperationException), plus an unused static logger field and an unused static import of AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE. This dead code should be removed (or wired in when token exchange is implemented for V2) to avoid confusion about how token-exchange evaluation is supposed to work in V2.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same unused private getEvaluationContext method in ClientPermissionsV2 and recommends removing it. The additional unused logger and import findings do not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Client deletion breaks with V2: listener calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled which throws UnsupportedOperationException

The registerListener handler now runs whenever Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled (which V2 depends on). On ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent it calls management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns the new ClientPermissionsV2, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled() unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). As a result, deleting any client in a realm with the V2 feature enabled will propagate a RuntimeException from the event listener and fail the client removal (and leave the client-specific authorization resources orphaned). The V2 path needs a no-op/cleanup implementation for client removal, or the listener must skip the clients() call for V2.

All-clients permission is ignored whenever a client-specific resource exists

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the all-clients ('Clients' resource type) fallback is only evaluated when resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), ...) returns null. If any client-specific resource exists for that client (e.g. another admin was granted a VIEW permission on that client, which creates the resource), the code evaluates only that resource's permissions and never considers permissions attached to the all-clients resource. An admin holding an all-clients MANAGE/VIEW/CONFIGURE permission would then be denied operations on that specific client, depending on which policies happen to reference the client-specific resource. Both the client-specific resource and the all-clients resource should be evaluated (granted if either matches), as in the V1 implementation where both the typed permission and the per-client permission are checked.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage access to admins holding only the 'view' scope on Groups

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the fallback checks hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), i.e. the VIEW scope alone satisfies canManage(). GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() guards group creation with auth.groups().requireManage(), so any admin who has been granted only the 'view' scope on the all-groups resource (or who matches a view permission) can create new top-level groups in the realm. canManage() should only check the MANAGE scope (compare canView() on line 52, which correctly checks VIEW and MANAGE).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect VIEW-or-MANAGE fallback in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), which allows VIEW-only users to obtain manage/write access. Both recommend checking only MANAGE; the candidate adds a concrete group-creation example.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() mixes up authorization Resource IDs with group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the callback passes groupResource.getId() (the authorization store Resource ID) into hasPermission(), which does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) — but per-group resources are named by the group ID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup/getOrCreateResource), so findByName with the Resource ID finds nothing and silently falls back to the all-groups resource evaluation. Worse, granted.add(groupResource.getId()) adds the Resource store ID, not the group ID. Callers (UsersResource.searchForUser, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser, UsersResource.getUsersCount) put this set into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute / count queries to filter users by group membership, so the filter uses non-existent group IDs and a fine-grained admin with view-members/manage-members permission on a group will see zero users instead of that group's members.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same resource-ID versus group-ID mismatch in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: resource IDs are passed to name-based permission lookup and returned for group membership filtering/counts, causing incorrect per-group permission evaluation and results.

false_positives.candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-groups resource does not exist

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(), when no per-group resource is found, resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) can return null (getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource is not found in the store, e.g. the admin-permissions client schema was not initialized for this resource server). The next line calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, causing a NullPointerException instead of cleanly denying access. UserPermissionsV2 has the same pattern, but there the 'Users' resource is guaranteed by V1 initialization; for the newly added Groups type the all-groups resource may not exist on older realms that enabled admin permissions before this schema change.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider services the default keystore type (e.g. the SUN provider), not a BouncyCastle provider. Callers of `CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` reasonably expect a BC/BCFIPS provider and may pass it into BC-specific APIs, which would fail or behave incorrectly in environments where this fallback provider is the one selected (i.e. standalone authz-client use). If no BouncyCastle provider is available, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or throwing would be less misleading.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies exactly the same issue: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider rather than a BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding (-1) is not handled, causing silent empty results or NegativeArraySizeException on malformed input

`readLength()` returns -1 for BER indefinite-length encoding (0x80). Callers do not handle this: `readSequence()` does `while (length > 0)` and silently returns an empty list for a -1 length (so `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` later fails with the misleading 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2'), and `readNext()` computes `length += reset()` and calls `read(length)` with a negative value, throwing an unhelpful `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of an IOException. Since this decoder parses signature bytes that ultimately come from a remote server, malformed/hostile input should produce a clear IOException. The -1 case should be rejected explicitly in `readLength()` (DER forbids indefinite lengths anyway) or handled by callers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify incorrect handling of the -1 length returned for indefinite-length encoding. The candidate describes downstream failures rather than the specific subtraction, but points to the same underlying bug: processing the sentinel as an ordinary length.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations

The PR adds `int order();` as a new abstract method to the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (the interface is in keycloak-common and is loaded via ServiceLoader precisely so it can be implemented externally) will now fail to compile, and existing compiled implementations will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` during sorting. This should be a `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) method to remain backward compatible.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate adds details about compilation failures, runtime AbstractMethodError, and a default-method fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple providers with equal order are now silently accepted, can select non-FIPS provider in FIPS setup

Previously, `detectProvider` threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which was a deliberate guard against misconfiguration. Now the code sorts by `order()` and silently picks the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200, and `Stream.sorted` is stable, so ties are resolved by arbitrary ServiceLoader enumeration order. If both the default (non-FIPS) and the FIPS 140-2 crypto jars end up on the classpath (a realistic packaging mistake), Keycloak will now silently start with whichever provider the classloader happens to return first — potentially the non-FIPS one in a FIPS-required environment — instead of failing fast. The previously ignored providers are only logged at debug level, so this misconfiguration is easy to miss. At minimum, equal-order ties among distinct providers should still be an error (or the FIPS provider should have a strictly higher order and a warning logged at WARN level).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() now returns null for a deleted group, risking NPE in callers that unbox the Long

The fix replaces the NPE inside getSubGroupsCount() with 'return model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount();'. While GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount accepts null, any other caller that unboxes the returned Long (e.g., arithmetic or comparison on getSubGroupsCount()) will now get a NullPointerException exactly in the concurrent-deletion scenario this PR is addressing. Other group model implementations never return null here (they return the actual count or 0), so returning 0 (or the cached subgroup set size) would preserve the contract more safely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that getSubGroupsCount() returning null violates its non-null contract and can cause NPEs in callers expecting a count, including callers that unbox the Long.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion races with in-flight reads

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti() starts a background thread that loops until deletedAll is set, then the main thread sets deletedAll.set(true) and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty without joining the thread. The reader thread can still be inside groups() when the assertion runs; an exception thrown by that final in-flight iteration is added to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already passed, so the regression this test is meant to catch can be silently missed (false positive). The thread should be joined before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the main thread sets deletedAll and asserts before waiting for the reader thread to finish, allowing exceptions from in-flight reads to be recorded after the assertion and missed.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared admin client used concurrently from two threads can produce unrelated failures

The reader thread and the main thread both use managedRealm.admin() (the same injected admin client / realm resource) concurrently. Keycloak's admin client is not thread-safe with respect to token refresh, so this test can fail intermittently for reasons unrelated to the NPE being fixed (e.g., concurrent token refresh errors recorded in caughtExceptions), making it flaky in CI. Consider using a separate admin client instance in the reader thread.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not match any declared method

`UsernameForm.authenticate` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only declaration added by this PR is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in `UsernamePasswordForm`. There is no no-arg overload in any changed file, so this does not compile. Presumably the intent was `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` (or a passkeys-enabled check without the user requirement, since at this point `context.getUser()` is known non-null, making the `user != null` check in the helper trivially true).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without the required UserModel argument, causing a method signature mismatch.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, so passkeys are never offered on a fresh (unauthenticated) login

The new helper `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Both call sites that replaced the old logic (`authenticate()` line 115 and `challenge(context, error, field)` line 137) previously filled the WebAuthn conditional-UI form data when the user was NOT yet set (`context.getUser() == null`) — that is the normal first-login case where passkey autofill (conditional UI) must be offered so the user can sign in with a discoverable credential. With the new condition, `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` only runs when a user is already set in the context (re-authentication), so on a fresh login the `webauth` form / challenge attributes are never rendered and users can no longer log in with passkeys at all. This is exactly the scenario covered by the updated tests asserting `//form[@id='webauth']` is present on the initial login page, which would now fail. The condition should allow the fresh-login case (user == null) as well as the re-authentication case, e.g. by not requiring `user != null` here.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same regression: requiring a non-null user prevents fillContextForm(context) from running on the initial login page, where no user is selected, breaking conditional UI for ID-less passkey authentication.

false_positives.candidate:
Overridden shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators missing @Override annotation

The newly added `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(AuthenticationFlowContext)` overrides the protected method introduced in `WebAuthnAuthenticator` but lacks the `@Override` annotation, so a future signature change in the parent would silently turn this into an unused method instead of a compile error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets are passed into queryset slicing, which Django rejects

The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django QuerySets explicitly do not support negative indexing: queryset[-5:95] raises ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). Cursor offsets come from the client-supplied cursor string (`value:offset:is_prev`), which Cursor.from_string parses with int() and no validation, so any user with the optimized_pagination flag can send a negative offset and get a 500. The 'advanced feature' is non-functional and only adds a new error path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: negative cursor offsets are used to slice Django QuerySets, which do not support negative slicing and raise an exception. The differing exception type does not change the issue identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError before the optimized branch

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences organization_context.member unconditionally for non-superusers. Requests authenticated without an organization membership context (e.g., certain token-based or org-auth-token flows that ControlSiloOrganizationEndpoint permits) have member=None, so this raises AttributeError and 500s the endpoint even though the user was never going to use the optimized path. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and ...` or getattr.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unguarded access to organization_context.member.has_global_access when member is None for token-authenticated requests, causing an AttributeError despite valid permissions. The candidate's different description of when the optimized path is used does not change the underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by datetime; it crashes on the first page

The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)` directly on the attribute value, which is a Python datetime object. math.floor/datetime raises TypeError (an integer is required). get_item_key is invoked by build_cursor on every result set (via _build_next_values/_build_prev_values), so the very first request using ?optimized_pagination=true will 500. This paginator needs the same epoch-milliseconds conversion DateTimePaginator performs (strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the audit logs endpoint paginates with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to a datetime value, causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
value_from_cursor returns a raw integer that is compared against a datetime column

Even ignoring the crash, OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns cursor.value unchanged (an integer), and build_queryset injects it into `WHERE <table>.datetime <= %s`. For a datetime-ordered queryset the cursor value must be converted back to a datetime (as DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does with fromtimestamp(value/1000)); comparing a datetime column to an integer epoch value will either error at the database level or silently match nothing/everything depending on coercion, corrupting pagination results.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets instead of rejecting them

The change to BasePaginator.get_result replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. A negative offset on a forward cursor previously raised a clear error; it is now silently treated as 0, so a client repeating a malformed/rewound cursor gets the first page again, which can cause infinite loops in polling consumers that keep following next cursors. Additionally, for is_prev cursors the raw (possibly negative) offset is still used in slicing and in the `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check, making that boundary check inconsistent with the clamped slice in the non-prev path.

No tests cover OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized audit log path

The PR adds ~100 lines of new pagination logic plus a new endpoint branch gated by query param and permissions, but no tests. Basic coverage (first page, next/prev cursor round trip, negative offset handling, non-privileged user requesting optimized_pagination, datetime ordering) would have immediately caught the math.floor(datetime) crash and the negative-slicing ValueError.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the whole-function lock allows concurrent BuildIndex for the same key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, which serialized index builds. Now the lock is only taken when inserting into the cache, so two concurrent callers can build an index for the same NamespacedResource simultaneously (e.g., getOrCreateIndex racing between a Search request and a watch event after init, since getOrCreateIndex has no per-key locking). For file-backed indexes both builds call bleve.New on the same directory, and the second one will fail because bleve locks the index directory; the loser also discards its work and one build silently overwrites the other in the cache. A per-key lock (singleflight) is needed to keep the speedup without allowing duplicate builds of the same key.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: narrowing b.cacheMu protection from the entire BuildIndex function to the cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to build the same expensive index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (RLock). Now that BuildIndex writes to b.cache concurrently (during parallel init and from watch-event-driven getOrCreateIndex builds), TotalDocs can run concurrently with a map write — init itself calls s.search.TotalDocs() while other builds may still be triggered by handleEvent. Concurrent map read/write is a fatal error in Go ("concurrent map read and map write"). Take b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while watcher-triggered BuildIndex operations may write to it concurrently, potentially causing a fatal concurrent map read/write error.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init

In searchSupport.init, each goroutine launched via group.Go executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, assigning to the `err` variable declared in the outer function scope. With s.initWorkers > 1, multiple goroutines write to this shared variable concurrently while group.Wait() and the surrounding code read it, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and return it: `_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`.

Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed from concurrent goroutines

totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside the errgroup goroutines (`totalBatchesIndexed++`) without any synchronization. With multiple init workers this is a concurrent read/write race and the final count reported in the tracing span event can be wrong. Use an atomic counter or increment outside the goroutines (e.g., from len(stats)).

NewResourceServer leaks the cancelable context and partially started watchers on Init failure

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns an error if it fails, but on that error path s.cancel() is never called. If search.init succeeded but initWatcher failed (or vice versa partially), the background watch goroutine(s) and poller started during init keep running with no way to stop them, since the constructor returned nil and the caller has no server handle to Stop. Call s.cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so the claimed 'natural backpressure' does not exist and the consumer can OOM

FixedQueuePool creates plain `queue.Queue()` instances with no maxsize, and `submit()` calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If processing is slower than consumption (the exact scenario this PR is designed to address — one slow item per queue), the queues grow without bound in memory, since the arroyo consumer keeps polling and submitting messages. The docstring on SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The consumer will buffer the entire topic backlog in-process and can be OOM-killed. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) so that `put` blocks the submit thread and actually applies backpressure.

FixedQueuePool is shut down permanently on strategy close, breaking the consumer after any partition rebalance

ResultsStrategyFactory creates the FixedQueuePool once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py line 133), and every call to `create_with_partitions` builds a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool. When partitions are revoked (rebalance), arroyo calls `close()` on the old strategy, which calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` — and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` is irreversible, plus `worker.shutdown = True` permanently stops the worker threads. On the next `create_with_partitions` after reassignment, the new strategy submits to shut-down queues whose workers have exited: messages will be accepted by `submit` (or raise `queue.ShutDown` from `put`) but never processed, stalling the consumer indefinitely with no errors. The pool must be created per-partition-assignment (in `create_with_partitions`) or restartable.

close() stops the commit thread before workers finish draining, so processed offsets are never committed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), the shutdown event is set and the commit thread is joined first, and only then is the queue pool shut down to drain. Any offsets completed by workers after the commit thread exits are never committed, and there is no final commit pass after the pool drains. On every shutdown/rebalance this silently reprocesses up to the last second-plus of already-handled messages; more importantly the pool's `worker.shutdown = True` flags mean items still sitting in the queues are dropped from memory entirely without their offsets ever being completed or committed. A graceful close should drain the queues, then run one final commit of get_committable_offsets() before joining the commit thread.

OffsetTracker retains offsets for revoked partitions forever and the commit loop may commit offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns

OffsetTracker never removes entries for partitions that are revoked during a rebalance — `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`last_committed` grow monotonically, and `_commit_loop` keeps calling `commit_function` (which is arroyo's commit callback for the current assignment) with committable offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own. Committing offsets for unassigned partitions is rejected by Kafka (or worse, commits a stale generation's offsets) and any remaining outstanding offset in a revoked partition will cause that partition to never advance in `get_committable_offsets`, keeping the tracker data alive forever. create_with_partitions/revocation should reset or prune per-partition tracking state.

Factory shutdown() sets queue_pool to None while strategies still reference it, and double-shutdown of a queue.Queue raises

ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and sets `self.queue_pool = None`, but any live SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by `create_with_partitions` still holds a reference to the pool and its `close()` will call `queue_pool.shutdown()` again. The second call invokes `queue.Queue.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down queue, which raises `queue.ShutDown`; the bare `except Exception` around `q.shutdown` in FixedQueuePool.swallows it, but the strategy's close ordering then becomes unpredictable. The factory and strategy both own pool lifecycle with no coordination — one of them should be responsible for shutdown.

submit() swallows all exceptions including grouping/serialization bugs and silently marks the offset complete, dropping messages

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), any exception from the decoder, `grouping_fn`, or `queue_pool.submit` is caught by the broad `except Exception` and the offset is added-then-completed, which makes it eligible to be committed. Unlike a decode failure (which legitimately returns None), a bug in `build_payload_grouping_key` or an internal error in pool submission now silently discards the message and commits past it with only a log line. For a Kafka consumer this converts transient/programming errors into permanent message loss rather than crashing or DLQ'ing. At minimum, non-decode failures should not mark the offset committable.

test_stats_reporting asserts queue is non-empty immediately after submit, which is inherently flaky

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. Since the pool's worker threads start consuming as soon as items are enqueued, on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before `get_stats()` runs, making this assertion fail nondeterministically. The same race applies to several uptime tests that poll `stats['total_items'] == 0 and call_count == N` — if a worker drains the queue before the mock records the call... actually those poll until a condition, so they are fine, but the immediate `> 0` assertion has no synchronization and will flake under load or with eager workers.

The script then does `hset main_redirect_key span_id set_span_id` and merges the span into whatever set that intermediate id resolves to, so a very deep segment tree gets split into two segments that are never rejoined (the old comment explicitly documented this failure mode at depth 10k). Additionally, evicted spans are dropped permanently with no metric, log, or outcome emitted, so data loss from oversized segments is invisible. The old behavior flushed oversized segments intact and only skipped them (with an error log and `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) when reading — that check was removed in buffer.py without a replacement, so `max_segment_spans` is now a dead constructor parameter and the only guard against huge segments is this silent truncation.

Because Check consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns Allowed=false immediately on a hit, a denial cached for an anonymous user on "dashboards:read" for some dashboard name will, for the next 30 seconds (shortCacheTTL), also deny the render service for the same action/name even though getRendererPermissions unconditionally grants render read access to dashboards/folders/datasources. If a user's permission is granted shortly after a denial was cached (e.g. a check raced ahead of the grant write for a just-created dashboard/folder, which is the exact scenario this PR is trying to fix), the user stays denied until the 30-second denial TTL expires, whereas the non-denial path would have picked up the new grant immediately via the DB fallback. false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole batch and skips all DB deletes

In the new cancellation section, all SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` calls are awaited sequentially inside a single try/catch, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises are only executed via `Promise.all` after the loop. If any single `client.request` throws (e.g. an invalid/expired batch_id, a reminder whose referenceId is null, or a transient SendGrid error), the catch fires and (a) all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are never cancelled at SendGrid, and (b) none of the reminder rows — including the ones that were successfully cancelled — are deleted from the DB. Those rows stay `cancelled: true` and are retried every 15 minutes, permanently failing behind the one bad record; meanwhile reminders whose scheduledDate passes before a successful run are removed by the top-of-handler deleteMany without ever being cancelled at SendGrid, so the email still goes out. Each reminder should be processed independently (try/catch inside the loop) and rows should be deleted once their cancellation succeeds.

remindersToCancel query missing method/scheduled filters

The query for reminders to cancel filters only on `cancelled: true` and scheduledDate, with no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` and no `scheduled: true` / `referenceId: { not: null }` constraint. Today only email reminders get `cancelled` set (SMS reminders are deleted immediately), but any SMS or unscheduled row that ever ends up with `cancelled: true` would be sent to SendGrid's scheduled_sends endpoint with a Twilio SID or null batch_id, which errors and — because of the shared try/catch — blocks cancellation of all legitimate email reminders in the same run. The query should restrict to scheduled email reminders with a non-null referenceId.

If processing is slower than consumption (the exact scenario this PR is designed to address — one slow item per queue), the queues grow without bound in memory, since the arroyo consumer keeps polling and submitting messages. In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), the shutdown event is set and the commit thread is joined first, and only then is the queue pool shut down to drain. On every shutdown/rebalance this silently reprocesses up to the last second-plus of already-handled messages; more importantly the pool's `worker.shutdown = True` flags mean items still sitting in the queues are dropped from memory entirely without their offsets ever being completed or committed. A graceful close should drain the queues, then run one final commit of get_committable_offsets() before joining the commit thread.

There is no metric, error, or fallback when the limit is hit, making the split silent. If the reduction was intentional for latency, the depth-limit-exceeded case should at least be observable.

The script now evicts with `zpopmin` whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. ZPOPMIN removes the lowest-scored members (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`), which may include the segment's root span — evicting it does not clear the `span-buf:hrs:` flag, so the segment will still be treated as having a root but will flush without one, producing an incomplete segment. Additionally, evicted spans are dropped permanently with no metric, log, or outcome emitted, so data loss from oversized segments is invisible. The old behavior flushed oversized segments intact and only skipped them (with an error log and `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) when reading — that check was removed in buffer.py without a replacement, so `max_segment_spans` is now a dead constructor parameter and the only guard against huge segments is this silent truncation.

The module docstring (and the glossary at line 58, "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys, containing span payloads") still describes the segment store as Redis sets and describes step 3 as adding payloads to a "set". After this change the keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and the redirect/merge logic in add-buffer.lua uses ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN. The stale documentation will mislead anyone reasoning about ordering, eviction, or the max-segment-size behavior.

This PR (titled/described as a spans buffer optimization) adds a new query parameter `optimized_pagination` to the audit log endpoint that switches pagination behavior based on a client-controlled flag, gated only on `is_superuser` or `member.has_global_access`. Aside from being broken (see OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime issue), it changes a public API contract with no tests, no changelog, and no relationship to the PR's stated purpose. It should be split out or removed.

The Kubernetes apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, and this function returns immediately after the storage write without waiting for the goroutine. As a result the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail with context.Canceled, silently dropping the legacy copy that mode 3 is supposed to maintain 'as a safe measure'. When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though no legacy call was made; the failure occurred in unified storage. The previous implementation fetched the old object once, computed the updated object, ran the storage update, and then wrote the storage-produced object (`obj`) to legacy via an `updateWrapper`, guaranteeing both stores converge to the same content. Since every real referer includes a path, the 'discourse-resize' message that app/assets/javascripts/embed.js relies on to size the iframe will never arrive, leaving the iframe at its default height. true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. Only href/src values starting with '/' are rewritten. Relative links like `href="page2.html"` or `src="images/pic.png"` are left untouched, so in imported topics they resolve relative to the forum's domain and produce broken links/images. Use URI.join(url, href) (or equivalent) for any non-absolute URL instead of only root-relative ones.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The downsize method is defined twice, and the second definition, which takes a dimensions argument, overrides the first, which takes max_width and max_height. true_positives.matched_candidate:

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)` routes animated GIFs (when `allow_animation` is true) to `downsize_instructions_animated`, which delegates to `resize_instructions_animated` producing `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80%` — gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects geometry like `WxH`, not a percentage, so the command fails and the GIF is never reduced (and the loop retries the same failing command 5 times).
